excerpt.span_text:
Ms. Sines. Thank you, Chairman Hawley and Ranking Member 
Durbin, and all of the other Senators on this Subcommittee. I 
am in front of you today during a time that will go down as a 
pivotal moment in fighting to protect our youth online.
    I was a freshman in high school in 2014 when I was 
approached by an online predator. He used the platform Facebook 
to first contact me and hid behind the account name called, 
``Closed Turn.''
    I remember that night. I was at TGI Fridays having dinner 
with my family. On the car ride home is when I opened the 
messages. He had stated that I had to get in contact with him. 
He immediately said that it was very important.
    At first, I ignored the messages. But he would only send 
more. I replied to the message, asking who this was, and they 
responded back, saying, I have something against you. You don't 
want anyone to see this. He had stated that he could not tell 
me what it was or who he had gotten it from. He told me that I 
couldn't tell anyone.
    He tricked me, making me believe that he already had 
compromising photos of me. In my teenaged brain, I panicked, 
and I thought I had no other choice but to comply with his 
orders. So, I did what I was told, and this began the torment 
that I endured.
    Despite his warnings not to tell anyone, I immediately 
disclosed to my school resource officer as soon as I got to 
school. He told me that there was nothing that he could do for 
me and to just ignore it and it would go away. He said that he 
couldn't help me in any way, even making me feel ashamed. He 
had no resources. He said he knew no one.
    After that, I thought there was nothing that anyone could 
do, especially because my school resource officer was a deputy 
from my local sheriff's department. If he's telling me that 
there is no one there to help, then it has to be true.
    After suffering for 2 years, I finally decided to take my 
voice back and share that I was being abused. The offender made 
good on his promises and took to Facebook to exploit me. He 
rapidly posted the hundreds of images and videos of me, making 
public pages and user accounts for more leverage. They were 
posted for the world to see.
    At that point, my family and I knew that we had to get law 
enforcement involved. We called 911, we explained what was 
happening, as my offender continued to post online.
    When an officer got to my house, we explained the 
situation, and I remember him looking at me and saying, look, 
I'm just a road deputy. I don't know much about this stuff. At 
this point, I had lost any hope that there was help. I had lost 
all hope that anyone even believed me.
    After a moment, he looked at me and he said, but I do know 
someone who may be able to help. Not much long after the phone 
call, there was a knock at my door--a detective who worked 
cybersecurity for the same department my school resource 
officer was from.
    As the detective and I sat in my kitchen and I shared my 
experience with him, he was on the phone with personnel from 
Facebook, attempting to get the content removed. We were told 
that the profiles, public pages, and content would not be taken 
down, as it did not violate their guidelines--guidelines that 
most companies still do not have in place. That was April of 
2016.
    It took time, and as we built connections within these 
platforms, we were able to get the content down within a few 
hours of the original postings, versus it taking a day or maybe 
a little bit longer to be taken off the platform.
    You have to understand, every minute, every second is 
filled with fear and anxiety for these victims. I consider 
myself lucky. Lucky that, in the end, I found a law enforcement 
agent who listened to me and who believed me. Lucky that my 
local State attorney offered a helping hand and, together, they 
set me up immediately with a trauma therapist. Lucky that they 
didn't give up. And it's because of their hard work that I get 
to sit in front of you today.
    I have connected with other survivors throughout the years, 
and I can tell you that my experience is rare. Not every victim 
has the same positive outcomes that I did. It took time from 
when I disclosed in April of 2016 to get to sentencing for my 
offender. He was eventually tracked down, as he masked his IP 
address, and arrested August 3 of 2017.
    From 2017 to 2021 was a back-and-forth of whether or not 
there would be a trial, or maybe we would get lucky and he 
would plead guilty. Finally, he pled guilty March 12, 2021. 
Four years ago from tomorrow is the day that he was sentenced 
to 75 years in Federal prison with no chance of parole. At the 
time of his sentencing, he had 375 other victims.
    The unique, unconsidered aspect of this crime is that we 
are trafficked right from our homes, right from our schools, 
from our communities. Anywhere that our cell phone goes with 
us, we can be trafficked.
    For these children, it feels that there is no escape and no 
end. While I no longer have content circulating the public web 
or any public platforms, my images could continue to be traded 
on the dark web. And what happens if they're ever publicly 
posted again?
    The STOP CSAM Act that is currently being considered will 
help ensure the safety of our children online and hold Big Tech 
accountable in reporting and protecting them while they use 
their platforms. The victim protections outlined in this bill 
will help others have a more positive experience with the 
criminal justice system overall.
    This bill could help give victims and survivors the 
opportunity to take back their lives and protect them from 
further victimization.
    Throughout my experience, I learned that this happened to 
me, not because of me, and it does not define me. Please help 
us continue the fight to protect our children online. Thank you 
for this opportunity.
